slides.title: A metric you did not check yourself is a claim, not a result
slides.statement: Running .fit() and reading a printed R² is not the same as knowing the number is right.
slides.supporting: Today's studio has one deliverable: verify the split, hand-compute a metric, diagnose the worst miss, and find AND fix a real leakage bug in AI-drafted code — the same bug shown in Meeting A, now yours to catch.

slides.title: [1] Load the portfolio, confirm 140 rows
slides.code:
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

DATA_PATH = Path("data") / "radley_portfolio_envelope.csv"
portfolio = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH, sep=",")
print(portfolio.shape)
slides.explainBody: eui_kwh_m2yr is the TARGET. wwr, shade_m, glazing_shgc are today's three FEATURES. est_annual_cost_index sits in the file too — reporting-only, never a feature (exactly today's bug).
slides.teaching: If (140, 9) does not print, stop and fix DATA_PATH before anything else — every later cell depends on this one.

slides.title: Predict: what prints when a verify-step assert passes?
slides.code:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

assert len(X_train) + len(X_test) == 140
assert set(X_train.index).isdisjoint(set(X_test.index))
slides.question: Both asserts pass. What prints to the console?
options: Nothing at all — a passing assert produces no output
An AssertionError, since nothing confirmed success
slides.why: assert only speaks when it FAILS — silence here IS "both checks passed." Confirmation needs your own print() line.
slides.teaching: Most students expect some kind of confirmation to print — naming this misconception before cell [2] runs prevents a real 'is it broken?' moment when nothing appears.

slides.title: [2] Verify the split — not just its shapes
slides.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

FEATURES3 = ["wwr", "shade_m", "glazing_shgc"]
X = portfolio[FEATURES3]
y = portfolio["eui_kwh_m2yr"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

print(X_train.shape, X_test.shape)
assert len(X_train) + len(X_test) == 140
assert set(X_train.index).isdisjoint(set(X_test.index))
slides.explainHead: Two real checks, not one printed shape
slides.explainBody: A set is a collection with no duplicates and no order — {1,2,3}.isdisjoint({4,5}) is True (nothing shared), {1,2,3}.isdisjoint({3,4}) is False. Converting each index to a set and calling .isdisjoint() asks one question: does ANY row-index number appear in both train and test? A correct-LOOKING shape can still hide overlap if code elsewhere re-samples the data — this is a DIFFERENT kind of leakage (rows, not columns) from cells [9]-[10]'s bug.
slides.teaching: Both asserts must run silently — no output at all means both passed. Ask what a raised AssertionError would mean here.

parts.body: Returns True only if the two sets share ZERO elements — a plain yes/no, not a count.

slides.title: [3] One documented helper, before any model
slides.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

def report_metrics(y_true, y_pred, label: str) -> dict:
    """Print and return MAE, RMSE and R2."""
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred))
    r2 = r2_score(y_true, y_pred)
    line = f"MAE={mae:.4f} RMSE={rmse:.4f} R2={r2:.5f}"
    print(label + ":", line)
    return {"MAE": mae, "RMSE": rmse, "R2": r2}
slides.explainHead: Four cells today score models — one function does it
slides.explainBody: Cells [3], [4], [9] and [10] all need the same three metrics. Writing the arithmetic four times is four chances to score two models differently. Note the convention required on every function since Week 4: a one-line docstring in triple quotes, plus type hints — label: str, -> dict. Nothing prints: defining a function only stores it.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment. Point at the docstring and both type hints by name before running — the handout requires this convention on every function students write from here to Project 2. R2 is printed to 5 decimals so the baseline's -0.00003 does not flatten to -0.0000.

slides.title: [3] continued: the naive baseline, scored by the helper
slides.code:
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor

baseline = DummyRegressor(strategy="mean")
baseline.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_b = baseline.predict(X_test)

print("predicts:", round(baseline.constant_[0][0], 4))
base = report_metrics(y_test, pred_b, "baseline")
slides.explainBody: If your printed numbers differ from 2.8906 / 3.8154 / -0.00003, check random_state=42 and FEATURES3 before moving on — everything downstream is judged against THESE three numbers. baseline.constant_[0][0] is the one value DummyRegressor predicts for every row: the training mean, 28.0836.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment: predicts 28.0836, MAE 2.8906, RMSE 3.8154, R2 -0.00003. Every model this session is judged against this exact baseline — write it on the board before cell [4] runs.

slides.title: [4] The AI-scaffolded fit — does it beat the baseline?
slides.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model3 = LinearRegression()
model3.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred_model3 = model3.predict(X_test)

print("coef_:", model3.coef_.round(4))
print("intercept_:", round(model3.intercept_, 4))
m3 = report_metrics(y_test, pred_model3, "3-feature")
slides.explainBody: Same coefficients as Meeting A — more window area raises EUI, more shading lowers it, higher SHGC raises it. Scored by the SAME helper as the baseline, so the comparison is exact, not approximate: MAE falls 2.8906 → 2.2680. R2=0.49374 still misses about half the variance; cell [7] names one honest reason why.
slides.teaching: Have students say aloud which sign they expected before revealing coef_ — this rehearses reading a coefficient's physical meaning.

slides.title: [5] Baseline vs. model — the required comparison
slides.callout: MAE improvement: (2.8906-2.2680)/2.8906 = 21.5%. The model beats the baseline — if it had not, that would be an equally real, equally reportable finding.
slides.teaching: This exact table, printed from your own run, IS the first required artifact of this week's graded studio assignment.

slides.title: Predict before cell [6] runs
slides.prompt: Cell [6] hand-computes MAE from its own definition — mean of |actual - predicted| — with no call to sklearn's function.
steps: State in one sentence what 'mean absolute error' should equal, in plain arithmetic terms.
Run cell [6] and read the first 8 printed rows.
Add up their |residual| values and divide by 8 — does your hand total roughly match the printed hand-added mean?
Confirm the FULL 35-row manual_mae equals 2.2680, matching cell [4] exactly.
slides.teaching: Expected hand-added mean of the first 8 rows: approx 1.82 — a smaller, different number from the full-sample MAE of 2.2680; both are correct, they are simply computed over different-sized subsets.

slides.title: [6] Calculate MAE manually — from its own definition
slides.code:
ids = portfolio.loc[X_test.index, "variant_id"].values
resid = (y_test.values - pred_model3).round(4)
residual_table = pd.DataFrame({"variant_id": ids,
    "actual": y_test.values, "predicted": pred_model3.round(4), "residual": resid})
print(residual_table.head(8))
manual_mae = np.mean(np.abs(resid))
print("manual MAE:", round(manual_mae, 4))
assert round(manual_mae, 2) == round(m3["MAE"], 2)
slides.output:
variant_id actual predicted residual
V109  23.71  26.2670  -2.5570
V068  23.35  24.0425  -0.6925
...(8 rows)
manual MAE: 2.268
slides.explainHead: No sklearn call — just np.abs and np.mean
slides.explainBody: MAE is 'add up how wrong every prediction was, ignoring direction, divide by how many.' Computing it this way, then asserting it equals cell [4]'s sklearn value, proves the FORMULA — not just the function — is understood.
slides.teaching: Have students hand-sum the printed 8-row subset with a calculator BEFORE running the full-sample manual_mae line — the two numbers (approx 1.82 vs 2.2680) are both correct, over different subsets.

slides.title: [7] Diagnose the largest residual
slides.code:
worst = residual_table.reindex(
    residual_table["residual"].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
print(worst.head(2))
row = portfolio.loc[portfolio["variant_id"] ==
    worst.iloc[0]["variant_id"]].iloc[0]
print(row[["wwr","shade_m","orientation"]])
slides.output:
variant_id  actual  predicted  residual
V037  20.43    26.7673   -6.3373
V133  23.05    27.9361   -4.8861
wwr             0.348
shade_m         0.917
orientation         N
Name: 36, dtype: object
slides.explainHead: V037: over-predicted by 6.34 — and here is why
slides.explainBody: reindex() here simply reorders residual_table's EXISTING rows into a new order — largest-to-smallest |residual| — it does not add, remove, or recompute any value. V037 has deep shading (0.917, among the deepest in the portfolio) AND north orientation — the coolest offset in the generating process. shade_m is IN the model (partial credit); orientation is NOT a numeric feature yet, so the model under-credits how well this design actually performs.
slides.teaching: Ask students to name the diagnosis in their own words before revealing this slide's explainBody — this is exactly the graded diagnosis step.

slides.title: [8] Residual plot — predicted vs. residual
slides.chartTitle: Test-set residual (actual - predicted) vs. predicted EUI
slides.explainHead: No obvious pattern — one clear outlier
slides.explainBody: Residuals scatter both above and below zero with no funnel or slope — the model's error does not grow or shrink systematically with the predicted value. V037 (-6.34) sits clearly apart from the rest, exactly the row diagnosed in cell [7].
slides.teaching: This is the identical chart data from Meeting A, now built by the student's own residual_table instead of read off a slide — point that out explicitly.

slides.title: Data leakage, recalled — check provenance, not plausibility

left.head: The definition
left.body: A feature that is (directly or nearly) DERIVED FROM the target — the model stops predicting and starts decoding the answer from a disguised copy of itself.

right.head: The provenance check
right.body: 'Cost is a design-relevant variable too' sounds plausible — that is exactly why leakage is dangerous. Asking 'how was this column COMPUTED?' catches what a plausibility read cannot.

slides.teaching: Remind students est_annual_cost_index correlates with eui_kwh_m2yr at 0.995574 — point back to Meeting A's exact number before running cell [9].

slides.title: Two kinds of leakage, not one
columns: how this studio just caught it
rows: the same row lands in both train AND test
a feature computed FROM the target — decodes, not predicts
slides.callout: Same word, two different bugs — row leakage breaks the SPLIT; column leakage breaks the FEATURE LIST. This studio's two checks catch each one separately, and neither check would catch the other.
slides.teaching: Point back at cell [2]'s explainBody, which named this contrast in passing — this slide gives it its own moment before cell [9] runs.

slides.title: [9] Run the AI-drafted 4-feature version yourself
slides.code:
FEATURES_LEAK = ["wwr", "shade_m", "glazing_shgc",
                 "est_annual_cost_index"]
X_leak = portfolio[FEATURES_LEAK]
Xtr_l, Xte_l, ytr_l, yte_l = train_test_split(
    X_leak, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
leak_model = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr_l, ytr_l)
pred_l = leak_model.predict(Xte_l)
print("coef_:", leak_model.coef_.round(4))
leak = report_metrics(yte_l, pred_l, "leaking")
corr = portfolio["est_annual_cost_index"].corr(y)
print("corr with target:", round(corr, 6))
slides.explainHead: R2=0.9923 is the red flag, before reading any code
slides.explainBody: Correlation ranges from -1 to 1; 0.995574 means the columns move almost in lockstep — suspicious for supposedly independent measurements. The original coefficients collapse while est_annual_cost_index's coefficient (7.1264) dominates. Provenance confirms the leak: est_annual_cost_index = eui_kwh_m2yr * 0.14 + small noise.
slides.teaching: Verified against the pinned course environment: coef_ [0.3310, 0.0374, 0.3054, 7.1264], MAE 0.2852, RMSE 0.3342, R2 0.99233 (0.9923 to 4 decimals), corr 0.995574 — matches data/README.md. Ask: would you have caught this by reading the code alone, without checking R2 or the correlation? Most students say no — that is the point of checking metrics AND provenance.

slides.title: [9] continued: turn “check the correlation” into a tool
slides.explainHead: One loop, one threshold, one list of suspects
slides.explainBody: The correlation you just typed by hand for ONE column becomes a loop over ANY feature list. abs(r) > 0.9 is a judgement call you are stating out loud, not a law: 0.9 is strict enough that no honest design variable in this portfolio trips it. {col:<22} left-aligns each name in 22 characters so the printed column of numbers stays readable.
slides.teaching: Freshly verified against the pinned course environment on radley_portfolio_envelope.csv. Nothing prints from this cell — it only defines the function. Ask students where the 0.9 came from before revealing that it is a stated choice, not a rule.

slides.title: ...continued: scan both feature lists, keep the tool
slides.code:
TARGET = "eui_kwh_m2yr"

suspects = leakage_scan(FEATURES_LEAK, TARGET)
print("suspects:", suspects)

for col in suspects:
    print("DROP:", col, "- derived from the target")
assert suspects == ["est_annual_cost_index"]
slides.output:
wwr                    corr=+0.5740
  shade_m                corr=-0.3481
  glazing_shgc           corr=+0.0128
  est_annual_cost_index  corr=+0.9956
suspects: ['est_annual_cost_index']
DROP: est_annual_cost_index - derived from the target
slides.explainBody: wwr (+0.5740), shade_m (-0.3481) and glazing_shgc (+0.0128) all correlate with EUI the way real design variables do — some strongly, some barely, none suspiciously. est_annual_cost_index sits at +0.9956, which is not what a measurement looks like; it is what a rescaled copy of the answer looks like. Keep this function: run it on your own Project 2 feature list before you fit anything.
slides.teaching: Freshly verified against the pinned course environment (new numbers, not in data/README.md, which only records the 0.995574 target correlation): wwr +0.5740, shade_m -0.3481, glazing_shgc +0.0128, est_annual_cost_index +0.9956. The assert passes silently — ask what its silence is claiming.

slides.title: Honest model vs. leaking model
slides.callout: R2 this close to 1.0 on a noisy, real-world-style target is the 'too good to be true' signal — be suspicious of a suspiciously perfect metric before you even look for the leaking column.
slides.teaching: Say this contrast is the entire audit in one table — an honest, imperfect model next to a suspiciously perfect one, same rows, same split.

slides.title: Watch the honest coefficients collapse
slides.chartTitle: wwr / shade_m / glazing_shgc coefficients, honest vs. leaking model
slides.explainBody: Every honest coefficient shrinks toward zero once est_annual_cost_index enters the model — not because wwr/shade_m/glazing_shgc stopped mattering, but because the leaking feature does almost all the work instead (its own coefficient, 7.1264, is off this chart's scale entirely).
slides.teaching: Point out this is the SAME two rows as the table two slides ago — a picture of the exact same collapse, not new data.

slides.title: Predict: what happens to MAE after the fix?
slides.code:
FEATURES_FIXED = ["wwr","shade_m","glazing_shgc"]
model_fixed = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr_f, ytr_f)
pred_f = model_fixed.predict(Xte_f)
fixed = report_metrics(yte_f, pred_f, "fixed")
slides.question: Same 3 features, same split. What MAE prints?
options: Somewhere between 2.2680 and 0.2852 — partial credit for trying the extra feature
Better than 2.2680 — the audit itself improves the model
Worse than 2.2680 — removing a feature always costs some accuracy
slides.why: Same 3 features, same split: this is cell [4]'s model again, to the decimal (MAE=2.2680) — REMOVAL is the fix, not a penalty.
slides.teaching: Many students expect SOME change, either better (for having 'fixed' something) or worse (for 'losing' a feature) — the identical-to-the-decimal result is the actual teaching point.

slides.title: [10] THE FIX — drop it, refit, prove it
slides.code:
FEATURES_FIXED = ["wwr", "shade_m", "glazing_shgc"]
assert "est_annual_cost_index" not in FEATURES_FIXED

X_fixed = portfolio[FEATURES_FIXED]
Xtr_f, Xte_f, ytr_f, yte_f = train_test_split(
    X_fixed, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
model_fixed = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr_f, ytr_f)
pred_f = model_fixed.predict(Xte_f)

fixed = report_metrics(yte_f, pred_f, "fixed")
assert round(fixed["MAE"], 4) == round(m3["MAE"], 4)
slides.explainHead: The fix is removal, not a smaller weight
slides.explainBody: Dropping est_annual_cost_index entirely — not down-weighting it — and refitting returns MAE/RMSE/R2 exactly to 2.2680 / 2.7146 / 0.49374. The final assert proves it: this IS the same honest model from cell [4], scored by the same helper, so the comparison cannot drift.
slides.teaching: This cell, run and passing silently, is the second required artifact of this week's graded studio assignment: the corrected code, with the bug explained.

slides.title: R2 across today's four models, in one picture
slides.chartTitle: R2 by model — baseline, honest, leak, fixed
slides.explainBody: R2 spikes to 0.9923 only because of the leaking feature — not because the model got smarter. Dropping it returns R2 to exactly 0.4937, the same honest number as earlier today: the real progress (baseline to 3-feature) stayed real, and the fake spike disappeared completely.
slides.teaching: This is literally today's whole studio arc, in one chart — use it to preview the closing slide's takeaways.

slides.title: Defend the fix in your own words
slides.prompt: An AI assistant argued 'cost is a design-relevant variable too' when it added est_annual_cost_index.
steps: State, in one sentence, what est_annual_cost_index is actually computed FROM.
Name the exact correlation value that confirms the leakage (from cell [9]).
Explain why 'plausible-sounding' is not the same test as 'legitimate feature.'
State the fix in one sentence, and the two metric values that confirm it worked.
slides.teaching: Expected answers: computed from eui_kwh_m2yr * 0.14 + noise; correlation 0.995574; plausibility is not provenance; fix = drop the feature, MAE/R2 return to 2.2680/0.4937.

slides.title: [11] Self-check: a different metric, a different row
slides.code:
manual_rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(residual_table["residual"]**2))
second_worst = worst.iloc[1]

assert round(manual_rmse, 2) == round(m3["RMSE"], 2)
assert second_worst["variant_id"] == "V133"
assert round(second_worst["residual"], 2) == -4.89
assert "est_annual_cost_index" not in FEATURES_FIXED
print("transfer check passed")
slides.explainHead: A different metric AND a different row — not a repeat
slides.explainBody: Cells [6]-[7] worked through MAE and V037 live. RMSE (which squares before averaging, penalizing large residuals more) on V133 (the SECOND-worst miss) proves the method generalizes, not just the one memorized answer.
slides.teaching: This is the required transfer check for this week's handout — point out it uses a genuinely different input than the live walkthrough, per the course's transfer-check policy.

      round(X_train["wwr"].min(), 3), "to",
      round(X_train["wwr"].max(), 3))
print("shade_m range in training data:",

Printing your own X_train min/max, once, is the one-line habit that catches a silent extrapolation yourself, on any model you fit, this week or in Project 2.

slides.teaching: This compiles as this week's graded weekly assignment — emphasize the four-heading cell structure is the rubric skeleton, matching every prior week's handout convention.

slides.title: Verified beats assumed, every time
takeaways: Checking a split's shapes is not the same as verifying it — an index-overlap assert is what proves no row leaked between train and test.
MAE computed by hand, from its own definition, matched sklearn's value to the decimal — 2.2680, both ways.
V037's -6.34 residual has a nameable cause (shading and orientation the model cannot see) — residuals are diagnosable, not random.
A suspiciously perfect R2 (0.9923) was the leakage signal itself; leakage_scan turns that one-off check into a tool you keep.
slides.teaching: Exit ticket: students name, in one sentence, the ONE check they will run first before trusting any new feature an AI assistant suggests next time.
